p.src: Now the two little demons held the counterfeit gourd in their hands and vied with each other to examine it. After a while, they looked up and found that the Pilgrim had vanished. Quick-witted Bug said, “Brother, even immortals tell lies. He said that after exchanging treasures he would help us become immortals, so why did he leave without a word?” Sharp-eyed Ghost said, “We got by far the better bargain. How could he possibly have escaped? Pass me the gourd. Let me put the sky into it and try it out.” He truly tossed the gourd upward, but down it fell with a thump. Quick-witted Bug cried in alarm, “Why did it not take it in? It did not take it in! Could Sun the Pilgrim have disguised himself as that immortal and traded this false gourd for our real one?” Sharp-eyed Ghost said, “Do not talk nonsense. Sun the Pilgrim was pinned beneath those three mountains. How could he get out? Give it here. Let me recite those few words of his spell and see whether it works.” The demon also tossed the little gourd into the air and recited, “If it refuses by so much as half a sound, I shall go up to the Hall of Miraculous Mist and raise a war.” Before he had finished, it fell down again with a thump. The two demons said, “It takes in nothing! It takes in nothing! It must be a fake.”

p.src: While they were making this commotion, the Great Sage Sun heard every word clearly and saw everything distinctly from midair. Fearing that if they kept fooling with it too long the secret might leak at the crucial moment, he shook himself and recalled to his body the hair that had become the gourd, leaving all four of the demons’ hands empty. Sharp-eyed Ghost said, “Brother, hand me the gourd.” Quick-witted Bug said, “You were holding it.” “Heavens! Where has it gone?” They groped wildly over the ground, searched madly through the grass, thrust their hands into their sleeves, and felt around their waists, but where could it be found? The two demons were scared witless and cried, “What are we to do? What are we to do? Our king entrusted the treasure to us and ordered us to capture Sun the Pilgrim. Now we have failed to capture the Pilgrim and even the treasure is gone. How dare we return to report? They will beat us straight to death. What are we to do! What are we to do?” Quick-witted Bug said, “Let us run away.” Sharp-eyed Ghost said, “Where would we go?” Quick-witted Bug said, “Anywhere at all. If we go back and say the treasure is gone, we shall certainly be sending ourselves to our deaths.” Sharp-eyed Ghost said, “Do not run. Let us go back. The Second King has always been fond of you. I shall put the blame on you with a few words. If he is willing to overlook it, our lives will be spared; if our excuses fail and we are beaten to death, at least we shall die here among our own. Let us not end up with nowhere to turn. Come, let us go. Come.” Having settled the matter, the demons turned back toward the mountain.

p.src: Seeing from midair that they were going back, the Pilgrim transformed himself once more, this time into a fly, and flew down to follow the little demons. But once he had become a fly, where did he put the treasures? Had he left them on the road or hidden them in the grass, someone might have seen and taken them, and then would not all his labor have been in vain? He still carried them on his person. Carried them on his person? A fly is no bigger than a bean; how could there be room? It turned out that those treasures, like his gold-banded staff, were wish-fulfilling Buddhist treasures that could change with their owner, becoming large or small at will, and thus could be carried on his body.

p.src: With a buzz he flew down and kept close behind the demons. Before long, they reached the cave. There sat the two demon chiefs drinking wine, and the little demons knelt before them. The Pilgrim alighted on the cabinet by the door and listened intently. The little demons said, “Your Majesties.” The two old demons immediately set down their cups and said, “You have returned?” The little demons replied, “We have.” They asked again, “Did you capture Sun the Pilgrim?” The little demons knocked their heads against the ground, not daring to utter a word. The old demons asked again, but still they dared not answer and only kowtowed. After being questioned repeatedly, the little demons prostrated themselves and said, “Mercy, Your Majesties, for crimes worthy of ten thousand deaths! Mercy for crimes worthy of ten thousand deaths! We took the treasures and had gone halfway down the mountain when we suddenly met an immortal from Mount Penglai. He asked where we were going, and we answered, ‘To capture Sun the Pilgrim.’ When the immortal heard the name Sun the Pilgrim, he said that he too bore him a grudge and wanted to help us. We did not ask for his help, but instead told him how our treasure could take people in. That immortal also had a gourd, one capable of taking in the sky. Thinking greedily of increasing our household wealth, we said: his takes in the sky, ours takes in people—why not trade with him? At first it was to be gourd for gourd, but Quick-witted Bug threw in the pure vase as well. Who would have thought that an immortal treasure could not bear the touch of mortal hands? Just as we were testing it, both the immortal and the treasure vanished. We beg Your Majesties to spare us from death.”

p.src: When the old demon heard this, he flew into a thunderous rage and cried, “It is all over! It is all over! That was Sun the Pilgrim disguised as an immortal, and he tricked you out of the treasures. That monkey has immense magical powers and friends everywhere. Some petty god must have released him, allowing him to cheat you of the treasures.” The second demon said, “Calm your anger, elder brother. That accursed monkey is truly outrageous! Since he had the skill to escape, he might simply have gone—why did he have to steal our treasures as well? If I lack the ability to capture him, I shall never again play the monster on the road to the West.” The old demon asked, “How will you capture him?” The second demon replied, “We had five treasures. Though two are gone, three remain, and with them we must capture him.” The old demon asked, “Which three remain?” The second demon replied, “I still have the Seven-Star Sword and the Plantain Fan with me, while the Golden Brocade Rope is kept by our old mother in Dragon-Subduing Cave on Dragon-Subduing Mountain. Let us now send two little demons to invite Mother here to eat Tang Monk’s flesh and tell her to bring the Golden Brocade Rope so that we may capture Sun the Pilgrim.” The old demon asked, “Whom shall we send?” The second demon replied, “We shall not send useless wretches like these.” With a shout, he ordered Sharp-eyed Ghost and Quick-witted Bug to rise. The two said, “What luck! What luck! We were neither beaten nor cursed, but pardoned just like that.” The second demon said, “Summon my regular attendants, Mountain-Straddling Tiger and Sea-Leaning Dragon.” The two knelt down, and the second demon instructed them, “You must be careful.” Both answered, “We shall be careful.” “You must be most attentive.” Both answered, “We shall be attentive.” He then asked, “Do you know the old lady’s home?” Again they both replied, “We do.” “Since you know it, set off early and quickly. When you reach the old lady, pay her our deepest respects and say that she is invited to eat Tang Monk’s flesh; and ask her to bring the Golden Brocade Rope so that we may capture Sun the Pilgrim.”

p.src: The two fiends received their orders and hurried away. Little did they know that the Pilgrim was nearby and had heard every word clearly. He spread his wings, flew after Bashanhu, caught up with him, and clung fast to his body. After they had gone two or three li, he was about to kill them both. Then he thought, “What difficulty would there be in killing them? But their old grandmother has the Golden Cord beside her, and I do not know where she lives. I had better question them first and kill them afterward.” Our fine Pilgrim gave a chirp, slipped away from the little fiend, and let him get a hundred paces or so ahead. Then, with a shake of his body, he changed into a little fiend himself. Wearing a fox-fur cap and hitching up his tiger-skin kilt backward around his waist, he caught up and called, “You fellows on the road, wait for me!” Yihailong turned and asked, “Where have you come from?” The Pilgrim said, “Good brother, do you not even recognize one of your own?” The little fiend said, “There is no one like you in our household.” The Pilgrim said, “How could I not belong? Take another good look at me.” The little fiend said, “Your face is unfamiliar—quite unfamiliar. We have never met.” The Pilgrim said, “Exactly. You have never met me because I serve in the outer detachment.” The little fiend said, “Then we truly have not met an officer of the outer detachment. Where are you going?” The Pilgrim said, “The kings said they had sent you two to invite the old grandmother to come and eat Tang Monk’s flesh, and told her to bring the Golden Cord to capture Sun the Pilgrim. Fearing that you might dawdle on the way, give yourselves over to play, and delay this important business, they sent me as well to urge you to hurry.”

p.src: Hearing him reveal this secret detail, the little fiends doubted him no longer and truly took the Pilgrim for one of their own. In frantic haste they raced ahead, covering another eight or nine li in a single burst. The Pilgrim said, “You are going rather too fast. How far are we from home now?” The little fiend said, “Fifteen or sixteen li.” The Pilgrim asked, “How much farther is it?” Pointing with his hand, Yihailong said, “It is right there in the Black Forest.” The Pilgrim looked up and saw a belt of dark woodland not far away. He reckoned that the old fiend must live somewhere in or around it. He stopped and let the little fiends walk ahead. Then he took out his iron staff, strode forward, and swept it at the backs of their legs. Pitifully frail as they were, a single blow mashed the two little fiends together into one cake of flesh. He dragged them by the feet and hid them in the deep grass beside the road. He then plucked out a hair, breathed an immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” The hair changed into Bashanhu, while he himself changed into Yihailong. Disguised as the two little fiends, they went straight to the Dragon-Subduing Cave to invite the old grandmother. Such was the vast divine power of the seventy-two transformations, and so sublime the art of making one thing serve as another.

p.src: In three or five strides they bounded into the forest. While searching about, he saw a pair of stone doors standing half open and half closed, but he dared not enter unbidden. He could only call out loudly, “Open the door! Open the door!” His cries promptly startled a female fiend guarding the entrance. She opened one leaf of the door and asked, “Where have you come from?” The Pilgrim said, “I have been sent from the Lotus-Flower Cave on Level-Top Mountain to invite the old grandmother.” The female fiend said, “Come in.” On reaching the second gateway, he craned his head and peered inside. p.src: When Great Sage Sun saw her, he dared not go in. He merely stood beyond the second gate with a glum face and began to weep outright. Why was he crying? Could he possibly have been afraid of her? Even if he had feared her, that would hardly have made him cry. Besides, he had already tricked her treasures away and killed her little fiends. Why, then, did he weep? Once, in former days, he had been cast into a nine-cauldron oil bath and fried for seven or eight days without shedding a single tear. He wept only because he had thought of the hardships Tang Monk suffered in seeking the scriptures. Anguish pierced his heart, and his tears poured freely. Inwardly he thought, “Since old Sun has displayed his art by changing into a little fiend and has come to invite this old monster, there is no reason I could simply stand upright and speak to her. She will surely expect me to kowtow. All my life I have played the hero, and I have bowed to only three people: in the Western Heaven, I bowed to the Buddha; in the Southern Sea, I bowed to Guanyin; and when Master rescued me at Double-Boundary Mountain, I bowed to him four times. For his sake I have racked every lobe of my lungs and liver, and exhausted every hair and hollow of my heart. How much can a single scroll of scripture be worth? Yet today I must bow to this monster. If I do not kneel and bow, I shall certainly give myself away. What misery! When all is said and done, it is only because Master is in peril that I must suffer humiliation at another’s hands.”

p.src: At this point there was nothing else he could do. He strode inside, knelt before her, and said, “Grandmother, I kowtow to you.” The monster said, “Rise, my child.” The Pilgrim said inwardly, “Fine, fine, fine! She has truly made me her son!” The old monster asked, “Where have you come from?” The Pilgrim replied, “By order of the two kings of the Lotus-Flower Cave on Level-Top Mountain, I have been sent to invite you, Grandmother, to come and eat Tang Monk’s flesh. They ask you to bring the Golden Cord as well, for they mean to capture Sun the Pilgrim.” Overjoyed, the old monster said, “What filial sons!” She immediately ordered them to bring out her sedan chair. The Pilgrim thought, “You wretch! So even fiends ride in sedan chairs?” From the rear quarters, two female fiends promptly carried out a fragrant rattan sedan chair, set it outside the door, and hung it with blue silk curtains. The old monster rose, left the cave, and seated herself inside the chair. Several young female fiends followed behind and alongside her, carrying a small dressing case, a mirror stand, a hand towel, and a box of incense. The old monster said, “Why are you coming along? I am going to my own sons’ home. Do you fear there will be no one there to attend me, that you must come fawning and currying favor? Go back, all of you. Shut the doors and mind the house.” The young fiends all went back as ordered, leaving only the two who bore the chair. The old monster asked, “What are the names of the two who were sent here?” The Pilgrim hastily answered, “He is called Bashanhu, and I am called Yihailong.” The old monster said, “You two walk ahead and clear the road for me.” The Pilgrim thought inwardly, “What rotten luck! I have not yet obtained the scriptures, yet here I am serving as her lackey.” Still, he dared not resist by force. He could only lead the way and raise the four great road-clearing cries.

p.src: After traveling some five or six li, he sat down on a rocky ledge and waited for the sedan bearers to catch up. Wukong said, “How about a short rest? The load is making my shoulder ache.” The little fiends knew nothing of his scheme and set down the sedan. Behind the sedan, Wukong plucked a hair from his chest, changed it into a great baked cake, and held it in both hands as he munched away. The bearers asked, “Officer, what are you eating?” Wukong replied, “It is a sorry tale. We have come all this long way to fetch your old madam, yet received not the least reward. I grew hungry, so I am eating some of the provisions I brought before we go on.” The bearers said, “Give us some to taste.” Wukong laughed. “Come along, then. We are all one family—why be stingy?” Knowing no better, the little fiends crowded around Wukong to share his provisions. Wukong whipped out his staff and swept it across their heads: one struck squarely was smashed to pulp; another merely grazed by it lay groaning, not yet dead. Hearing someone groan, the old fiend poked her head out of the sedan to look. Wukong sprang before her and brought his staff down upon her crown, smashing a hole in it so that brains spurted and fresh blood gushed forth. When he dragged her from the sedan and looked, she proved to be a nine-tailed fox. Wukong laughed. “You sinful beast! What do you mean by calling yourself the old madam? If you are the old madam, then you ought to address Old Sun as your supreme ancestral grandsire!”

We have come all this long way to fetch your old madam, yet received not the least reward. I grew hungry, so I am eating some of the provisions I brought before we go on.”
The bearers said, “Give us some to taste.”
Wukong laughed. “Come along, then. We are all one family—why be stingy?”
Knowing no better, the little fiends crowded around Wukong to share his provisions.
Wukong whipped out his staff and swept it across their heads: one struck squarely was smashed to pulp;
another merely grazed by it lay groaning, not yet dead.

Hearing someone groan, the old fiend poked her head out of the sedan to look. Wukong sprang before her and brought his staff down upon her crown, smashing a hole in it so that brains spurted and fresh blood gushed forth.
When he dragged her from the sedan and looked, she proved to be a nine-tailed fox.
Wukong laughed. “You sinful beast! What do you mean by calling yourself the old madam?
If you are the old madam, then you ought to address Old Sun as your supreme ancestral grandsire!”

p.src: The fine Monkey King searched her body, found the Gold-Brocade Rope, and tucked it into his sleeve. Delighted, he said, “Whatever powers those wretched demons may possess, three of their treasures now bear the name of Sun.” He then plucked two more hairs and changed them into Bashanhu and Yihailong; he plucked another two and changed them into a pair of sedan bearers; while he himself assumed the old madam’s appearance and sat inside the sedan. They raised the sedan and went straight back along the road by which they had come.

p.src: Before long they reached the entrance to Lotus Cave. The little fiends transformed from hairs called out in front, “Open the gate! Open the gate!” A gatekeeping fiend inside opened up and asked, “Have Bashanhu and Yihailong returned?” The hairs replied, “We have.” “And where is the old madam you were sent to fetch?” The hairs pointed and said, “Is that not she inside the sedan?” The little fiend said, “Wait here while I go in and announce her arrival.” He reported, “Great Kings, the old madam has arrived!” On hearing this, the two demon chiefs immediately ordered an incense table prepared to welcome her. Wukong heard this and rejoiced inwardly. “What luck! At last it is my turn to be treated like somebody. When I changed into a little fiend and went to fetch the old monster, I had to kowtow once to her; this time I am disguised as the old monster and am their mother, so they are bound to perform the four obeisances. It may not amount to much, but at least I shall win two kowtows from each of them.” The great Sage stepped out of the sedan, shook out his clothes, and took the four hairs back onto his body. The gatekeeping fiends carried the empty sedan inside. He followed slowly behind, mincing and simpering with coy affectation, imitating the old monster’s every movement as he went straight inside. There he saw all the fiends, great and small, come forward and kneel in welcome. Drums, pipes, and stately music rang out in a brilliant chorus; from the Boshan incense burner curled dense, fragrant smoke. He entered the main hall and sat facing south. The two demon chiefs dropped to both knees, kowtowed before him, and cried, “Mother, your sons salute you.” Wukong said, “Rise, my sons.”

p.src: Now Zhu Bajie, hanging from a beam, suddenly gave a loud laugh. Sha Monk said, “Second Elder Brother, this is fine indeed—you have been hanging there so long you have started laughing!” Bajie said, “Brother, I have a reason for laughing.” Sha Monk asked, “What reason?” Bajie said, “We feared that once the old madam arrived, we would be steamed and eaten. But it turns out that it is no old madam—an old familiar tale has arrived instead.” Sha Monk asked, “What old tale?” Bajie laughed. “The Protector of the Horses is here.” Sha Monk asked, “How do you know it is he?” Bajie replied, “When she bent down and said, ‘Rise, my sons,’ a monkey’s tail stuck up behind her. I am hanging higher than you, so I saw it clearly.” Sha Monk said, “Keep quiet for now. Let us hear what he has to say.” Bajie said, “Quite right, quite right.”

p.src: The Great Sage Sun sat in the middle and asked, “My sons, for what purpose have you invited me here?” The demon chiefs replied, “Mother, your sons have lately been remiss in courtesy and have had no chance to show our filial devotion. This morning, we foolish brothers captured the Tang monk from the Eastern Land. We dared not eat him on our own, so we invited Mother here to enjoy him fresh. We shall steam him for you to eat and prolong your life.” Wukong said, “My sons, I have no desire to eat the Tang monk’s flesh. I hear that Zhu Bajie’s ears are excellent, though. Cut them off and prepare them nicely as a relish for my wine.” Hearing this, Bajie panicked and cried, “Damn you! So you came here to cut off my ears! If I shout out, you will not like the sound of it!”

p.src: Alas! That single knowing remark from the fool gave away the secret of the Monkey King’s transformation. Just then several fiends who had been patrolling the mountain, together with the gate guards, came crashing in and reported, “Great Kings, disaster! Sun Wukong killed the old madam and has come here disguised as her!” The demon chiefs heard this and, allowing no explanation, drew the Seven-Star Precious Sword and slashed straight at Wukong’s face. But the great Sage shook his body; a red radiance filled the entire cave, and he had already escaped. Such tricks as these were splendid sport indeed. Truly, gathered together he took form; dispersed, he became vapor.

p.src: The elder demon chief was so frightened that his soul fled and his wits scattered, while all the fiends bit their fingers and shook their heads. The elder demon said, “Brother, return the Tang monk, Sha Monk, Bajie, the white horse, and all the luggage to Sun Wukong. Let us close the door on this quarrel.” The second demon replied, “Brother, what are you saying? Who knows how much toil I spent devising this scheme and capturing all those monks? If, merely because you fear Sun Wukong’s cunning, we now send them all back to him, we shall truly be men who shrink from blades and flee from swords. How could that be the conduct of a true hero? Please sit down and have no fear. I have heard you say that Sun Wukong possesses immense magic powers. Though I have encountered him once, I have never actually tested my skill against his. Bring me my armor. I shall seek him out and fight him for three bouts. If he cannot defeat me in three bouts, the Tang monk shall remain our food; if I cannot defeat him in three, it will not be too late then to return the Tang monk to him.” The elder demon said, “You are right, worthy brother.” He ordered the armor brought out.

p.src: The second demon shouted, “Sun Wukong, quickly return my treasures and my mother! Then I shall let your Tang monk go fetch the scriptures.” Unable to contain himself, the great Sage cursed, “You wretched monster! You have mistaken your Grandpa Sun. Return my master, my fellow disciples, the white horse, and the luggage without delay, give me some travel money besides, and send us on our westward journey. If even half the word ‘no’ passes between your teeth, go twist yourself a rope. That will save your grandpa the trouble of laying hands on you.” Hearing this, the second demon swiftly mounted a cloud, leaped into the air, and swung his precious sword to thrust at him; Wukong drew his iron staff and met him head-on. The two fought in midair—a splendid battle it was:

p.src: Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly, thinking, “This wretched fiend can indeed withstand Old Sun’s iron staff. I have already obtained three of his treasures; if I keep struggling so bitterly against him, won’t I merely waste my time? Would it not be far better to put him into the gourd or the pure vase?” Then he thought, “No, that won’t do. As the saying goes, ‘A thing obeys its master.’ If I call him and he does not answer, won’t that spoil the whole affair? I had better snare him with the Golden-Brocade Rope.” The Great Sage, resourceful as ever, wielded his staff with one hand to parry the fiend’s weapon, while with the other he raised the rope and, with a swish, slipped it over the fiend’s head.

p.src: Now the fiend possessed both a spell for tightening the rope and one for loosening it. When the rope caught an enemy, he recited the tightening spell, and none could escape; when it caught one of his own, he recited the loosening spell so that no harm would come to him. Recognizing his own treasure, he recited the loosening spell. The rope slackened, and he slipped free; then he flung it back at Pilgrim, and in an instant it had snared the Great Sage. The Great Sage was about to use his body-shrinking magic to escape, but the fiend recited the tightening spell, binding him fast. How could he possibly get free? When it slipped down below his neck, it proved to be a golden ring encircling him. The fiend gave the rope a tug and pulled him down, then struck his bare head seven or eight times with his precious sword. Not even the skin of Pilgrim’s head turned the slightest shade of red. The fiend said, “Monkey, since your head is so hard, I shall not cut you anymore. I’ll take you back and beat you there. Now return my two treasures at once.” Pilgrim said, “What treasure of yours have I taken, that you should demand it from me?” The fiend searched him carefully from head to foot and found both the gourd and the pure vase. Leading him by the rope into the cave, he announced, “Elder Brother, I have brought him.” The elder fiend asked, “Whom have you captured?” The second fiend replied, “Sun the Pilgrim. Come and see, come and see.” At one glance the elder fiend recognized Pilgrim and exclaimed with a broad smile, “It is he! It is he! Tie him to the pillar with a long length of rope, for our amusement.” They duly tied Pilgrim fast, and the two fiends went into the rear hall to drink.

p.src: As the Great Sage writhed and struggled at the foot of the pillar, he suddenly roused Bajie. The idiot, hanging from a beam, laughed aloud and said, “Brother, it seems you won’t get to eat my ears after all.” Pilgrim said, “Idiot, are you enjoying yourself up there? I shall get out at once, and I promise I will rescue all of you.” Bajie said, “Have you no shame? No shame at all! You cannot even free yourself, yet you still talk of rescuing others. Enough, enough! Let master and disciples all die together, so we can ask one another the way in the Realm of Shades.” Pilgrim said, “Stop talking nonsense and watch me get out.” Bajie replied, “I would like to see how you manage it.” While the Great Sage spoke with Bajie, his eyes remained fixed on the two fiends. He saw them drinking inside while several lesser fiends, bearing trays and cups, carried pots and poured wine, hurrying endlessly to and fro. Their guard had relaxed a little. Seeing no one before him, he exercised his magic: he drew out his staff, breathed an immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It instantly became a file of solid steel. He pulled the ring around his neck into reach and, after a few strokes of the file, cut it into two pieces. He pried open the cut and slipped free. Then he plucked a hair and changed it into a false likeness of himself, which he tied there in his place. His true body gave a shake, transformed into a lesser fiend, and stood nearby. Bajie cried again from the beam, “Disaster! Disaster! The one tied up is a counterfeit, while the one hanging here is the genuine article!” The elder fiend set down his cup and asked, “What is that Zhu Bajie shouting about?” Pilgrim, already transformed into a lesser fiend, stepped forward and said, “Zhu Bajie is urging Sun the Pilgrim to escape by transformation, but Sun refuses to go, so Bajie is shouting at him.” The second fiend said, “People claim Zhu Bajie is honest, but he is nothing of the sort. He deserves more than twenty blows across the mouth.”

I know who you are.” Pilgrim said, “Old Sun transformed himself solely for your sake, yet you nearly gave me away! Not one of the fiends in this whole cave recognized me. Why were you alone able to do so?” Bajie replied, “Though you changed your face and head, you forgot to change your backside. Are there not two red patches on your rump? That is how I knew it was you.” Pilgrim slipped into the rear, made his way to the kitchen, and scooped up a handful of soot from beneath the stove. He blackened both buttocks with it and returned to the front. When Bajie saw him, he laughed again and said, “Where has that monkey been messing about all this time, to come back with a black backside?”

p.src: Pilgrim remained close at hand, intent on stealing the fiends’ treasure. He was truly resourceful. Going up into the hall, he bowed with one leg extended and said to the fiend, “Great King, look at that Sun the Pilgrim writhing and struggling against the pillar. He will wear through that golden rope. It would be best to replace it with a stouter rope.” The elder fiend said, “You are right.” He immediately untied the lion-patterned belt from his waist and handed it to Pilgrim. Pilgrim took the belt and used it to bind the counterfeit Pilgrim. He removed the other rope and coiled it neatly inside his sleeve. Then he plucked another hair, breathed an immortal breath upon it, and changed it into a false Golden-Brocade Rope, which he presented to the fiend with both hands. The fiend, being wholly absorbed in drinking, never examined it closely and simply took it back. Such was the Great Sage’s art of substitution: once again, a single hair had been exchanged for the Golden-Brocade Rope.

p.src: Having secured the treasure, he hurriedly turned, sprang out through the gate, resumed his true form, and shouted, “Monsters!” The little demon guarding the gate asked, “Who are you, to make such an uproar here?” Pilgrim said, “Hurry inside and report to that wretched fiend of yours that Zhexingsun has come.” The little demon went in and reported as instructed. Greatly startled, the elder demon said, “We captured Sun Wukong—how can there now be a Zhexingsun?” The second demon said, “Brother, what is there to fear from him? All the treasures are in my hands. Let me take the gourd outside and draw him into it.” The elder demon said, “Be careful, brother.” The second demon took the gourd and walked out through the mountain gate. There he suddenly saw someone identical in appearance to Sun Wukong, only a little shorter. He asked, “Where have you come from?” Pilgrim replied, “I am Sun Wukong’s brother. I heard that you captured my elder brother, so I have come to settle the score with you.” The second demon said, “I did capture him, and he is chained up inside the cave. Since you have come here, you must mean to challenge me. But I will not fight you. I shall merely call your name—do you dare answer me?” Pilgrim said, “You may call me a thousand times, and I will answer you ten thousand!” Gripping the treasure, the demon leapt into the air, turned its base toward the sky and its mouth toward the earth, and called, “Zhexingsun!” Pilgrim dared not answer. He thought to himself, “If I answer, I will be sucked inside.” The demon said, “Why do you not answer me?” Pilgrim replied, “My hearing is a little poor; I did not hear you. Call louder.” The monster called again, “Zhexingsun!” Down below, Pilgrim counted on his fingers and said, “My real name is Sun Wukong, while Zhexingsun is a sham name I made up. It may be able to draw in a real name, but surely it cannot draw in a false one.” Unable to restrain himself, he answered the call. Whoosh! The demon sucked him into the gourd and affixed the seal. As it happened, the treasure cared nothing for whether a name was true or false: the merest breath of an answer was enough for it to draw a person inside.

Pilgrim said, “You may call me a thousand times, and I will answer you ten thousand!”
Gripping the treasure, the demon leapt into the air, turned its base toward the sky and its mouth toward the earth, and called, “Zhexingsun!”
Pilgrim dared not answer. He thought to himself, “If I answer, I will be sucked inside.”
The demon said, “Why do you not answer me?”
Pilgrim replied, “My hearing is a little poor; I did not hear you.
Call louder.”
The monster called again, “Zhexingsun!”
Down below, Pilgrim counted on his fingers and said, “My real name is Sun Wukong, while Zhexingsun is a sham name I made up.
It may be able to draw in a real name, but surely it cannot draw in a false one.”
Unable to restrain himself, he answered the call.
Whoosh! The demon sucked him into the gourd and affixed the seal.
As it happened, the treasure cared nothing for whether a name was true or false: the merest breath of an answer was enough for it to draw a person inside.

p.src: Inside the gourd, the Great Sage found himself surrounded by utter darkness. He thrust his head upward, but could not budge the stopper, which was wedged extremely tight. Only then did he grow anxious and think, “When I met those two little demons on the mountain, they told me that whether a person was put into the gourd or the pure-jade vase, it took only an hour and three quarters to dissolve him into pus. Could it possibly dissolve me too?” Then another thought came to him: “No matter. It cannot dissolve me. Five hundred years ago, when I, Old Sun, wreaked havoc in Heaven, the Supreme Lord Lao placed me in the Eight-Trigram Furnace and refined me for forty-nine days. That forged me a heart and liver of gold, lungs and entrails of silver, a copper head and iron back, and fiery eyes with golden pupils. How could I be dissolved in a mere hour and three quarters? For now I shall go inside with him and see what he does.”

p.src: The second demon carried the gourd inside and said, “Brother, I have caught him.” The elder demon asked, “Whom did you catch?” The second demon said, “I have Zhexingsun shut inside the gourd.” Delighted, the elder demon said, “Worthy brother, take a seat. Do not disturb it. Wait until it rattles when shaken before removing the seal.” Hearing this, Pilgrim thought, “With a body like mine, how could I possibly rattle when shaken? Only after I have dissolved into thin liquid would I make a sound. I had better urinate. When they hear it sloshing, they will surely remove the seal and lift the lid, and I can seize the chance to escape from the bastards.” Then he thought again, “No, no. Urine would make a sound, but it would soil my robe. When they shake the gourd, I shall merely gather some saliva and swill it around noisily in my mouth. That will trick them into opening it, and then I, Old Sun, can escape.” The Great Sage made his preparations, but the monster was too intent on drinking to shake the gourd. The Great Sage worked a spell, intending only to induce him to shake it, and suddenly cried, “Heavens! My ankle bones have dissolved!” Still the demon did not shake it. The Great Sage cried again, “Mother! Even the bones across my waist have dissolved!” The elder demon said, “Once it has dissolved up to the waist, the rest will all be gone. Remove the seal and have a look.”

p.src: On hearing this, the Great Sage plucked out a hair and cried, “Change!” It changed into the lower half of a body and lay at the bottom of the gourd. His true body changed into a tiny insect and clung beside the mouth of the gourd. The instant the second demon lifted the seal to look inside, the Great Sage flew out. He rolled over and changed again, this time into Yihailong. Yihailong was the little demon originally sent to invite the old lady. Having assumed his form, Pilgrim stood to one side. The elder demon pulled open the mouth of the gourd and peered inside. Seeing half a body still twitching, he could not tell whether it was genuine or false and hurriedly cried, “Brother, close it! Close it! He has not completely dissolved yet!” The second demon replaced the seal as before. Standing nearby, the Great Sage laughed inwardly and thought, “Little do they know that Old Sun is already out here.”

p.src: The elder demon took up the winepot, filled a cup to the brim, approached the second demon, and offered it with both hands, saying, “Worthy brother, let me offer you a cup.” The second demon said, “Elder brother, we have already been drinking for quite some time. Why offer me another cup?” The elder demon said, “Capturing Tang Sanzang, Bajie, and Sha Seng would have been achievement enough, yet you also demanded Sun Wukong’s return and trapped Zhexingsun. For such great merit, I ought to offer you several more cups.” Seeing his brother treat him with such respect, the second demon dared not refuse. But as one hand supported the gourd, he could not receive the cup properly, so he handed the gourd to Yihailong and accepted the wine with both hands. He did not know that this Yihailong was Sun Wukong in disguise. See how attentively Pilgrim held the gourd and waited upon them. After accepting and drinking the wine, the second demon wished to return the courtesy with a cup of his own. The elder demon said, “There is no need to return the cup. I shall simply drink one with you here.” The two continued exchanging courtesies. With the gourd balanced on his head, Pilgrim watched them intently as they passed cups back and forth, utterly unsuspecting. He slipped the gourd into his sleeve. He plucked out a hair, changed it into a false gourd identical to the original, and held it in his hands. After the demons had exchanged wine for a while, the second demon took back the treasure without checking whether it was real or false. Each returned to his place at the feast, sat down at ease, and resumed drinking. The Great Sage Sun withdrew and slipped away. Delighted to have obtained the treasure, he thought, “However capable that fiend may be, in the end this gourd still belongs to Sun.”
